summaries.example: Imagine a box of rule cards. One card says, “If it is raining, the ground is wet.” Another says, “It is raining.” We can use the cards to reach “The ground is wet.” A logic studies when a conclusion really follows from starting statements. Algebraic logic gives the statements values and operations, much like a number system gives numbers ways to be combined. If the rules and the value system agree, the value system helps us understand the logic.
summaries.summary: Algebraic propositional logic studies a broad question: how can mathematical structures help us understand systems of reasoning? A logic has a language, made from variables and connectives such as “and,” “or,” and “if…then.” It also has rules saying when a conclusion follows from premises. The source explains that this idea of consequence is more useful for general study than looking only at theorems, which are conclusions proved with no extra premises. Logics may be described by proofs, by models, or by both. In classical logic, truth tables determine whether a conclusion follows. Other systems, such as intuitionistic and modal logics, use different rules or meanings. Algebraic logic treats formulas as if they were expressions built by operations. An algebra gives meanings to those operations, and a chosen set of values can count as “designated,” or acceptable. A logical matrix combines an algebra with such a set. The main goal is to discover how properties of a logic match properties of its algebras. Sometimes the connection is especially strong: a logic is then called algebraizable. The source also explains that not every logic has this strongest connection, so researchers use broader tools, including logical matrices and generalized matrices.
key_ideas: Logic can be described by what conclusions follow from given premises.
A consequence relation should keep track of basic rules such as using a premise, adding more premises, and using a finite part of a large set when appropriate.
Different logics can use different rules. Classical, intuitionistic, modal, linear, and relevance logics are examples.
Algebraic logic studies a logic by connecting its formulas with algebras and other mathematical structures.
A proof system and a semantic system can be compared: soundness means proofs do not lead to wrong semantic conclusions, while completeness means the semantic conclusions can also be proved.
summaries.why_it_matters: This subject shows that reasoning can be studied in more than one way. A proof tells us how to reach a conclusion, while a mathematical model helps explain why the conclusion is valid. Comparing these viewpoints can reveal what different logics share and where they differ. These ideas also support work in mathematics and computer science, where rules must be checked carefully.

important_terms.definition: A starting statement or group of statements used to support a conclusion.
A statement that follows from one or more premises according to some rules.
A mathematical structure with a collection of things and operations for combining them.
A way to check whether conclusions follow, using values or mathematical structures.
A pair made from an algebra and a chosen set of values that count as acceptable.

questions_to_think_about: If you add another true clue to a puzzle, should a conclusion you already had stop following?
Why might people want more than one kind of logic?
How is a truth table like a small machine for checking rules?
Can two different mathematical structures help explain the same logic?

summaries.example: Consider two modal systems using the same symbols, including □ for “necessarily” or “in every relevant situation.” In a global version of a normal modal logic, the premise p can lead to □p. In the local version, p does not generally lead to □p. Thus two systems may use the same language and have the same theorems while differing in what follows from nonempty sets of premises. Their algebraic behavior can therefore differ as well.
summaries.summary: The entry introduces Abstract Algebraic Logic, a general study of propositional logics through algebraic structures. Its organizing idea is logical consequence: a relation between premises and conclusions satisfying structural conditions. A logic is not merely a collection of theorems; it includes a formal language and a substitution-invariant consequence relation. The same relation may be defined syntactically by axioms and inference rules or semantically through mathematical models. A proof system is sound for a semantics when everything provable is semantically valid, and complete when every semantically valid consequence is provable. To algebraize a propositional language, formulas are viewed as terms, while connectives become operations in an algebra. A logical matrix adds a set of designated elements to an algebra, allowing semantics even when designated values cannot be defined by equations alone. The Leibniz congruence identifies algebraic elements that the matrix cannot distinguish in their logical behavior. Reduced matrices remove this redundancy. The Lindenbaum-Tarski method uses theories and quotient algebras of formulas to construct semantic models and prove completeness. In the best-behaved cases, a logic is algebraizable: formulas translate into defining equations, equations translate back through equivalence formulas, and the associated algebraic class reflects important logical properties. However, the local and global forms of normal modal logic K illustrate that sharing an algebraic counterpart does not guarantee sharing all logical features. The entry therefore also discusses broader classifications, including protoalgebraic, equivalential, selfextensional, and Fregean logics, as well as generalized matrices for logics not handled adequately by a one
key_ideas: Tarski’s abstract notion of consequence treats deduction as an operation assigning consequences to sets of premises. Finitary consequence depends on finite subsets.

A propositional logic consists of a language and a structural consequence relation. It may be presented syntactically by calculi or semantically by algebras, matrices, Kripke models, or related structures.
Algebraic semantics interprets formulas as terms and connectives as operations. Designated elements specify which algebraic values count as acceptable.
Soundness and completeness connect proof systems with semantics. The Lindenbaum-Tarski method builds quotient algebras from theories to establish completeness in important cases.
Classical logic corresponds to Boolean algebras and intuitionistic logic to Heyting algebras in their standard algebraic semantics.

Algebraizability is stronger than merely having some algebraic semantics. It requires mutually informative translations between formulas and equations, using defining equations and equivalence formulas.
summaries.why_it_matters: Algebraic logic clarifies the relationship between reasoning rules and mathematical models. This matters whenever we want to know whether a formal system is reliable, whether a semantic description captures all proofs, or why two systems with similar notation behave differently. It also provides a common framework for studying classical and non-classical logics rather than treating each as an isolated subject.

important_terms.definition: A relation between sets of formulas and formulas that specifies when a conclusion follows from premises and satisfies structural rules such as reflexivity and transitivity.
A logic whose consequence relation is unchanged when formulas are uniformly substituted for propositional variables.
A mathematical structure interpreting each connective as an operation on a set; formulas can be evaluated in it.
A pair consisting of an algebra and a set of designated elements; premises and conclusions must evaluate into the designated set.
A congruence that identifies algebraic elements that cannot be distinguished by the designated set through formulas.
A logic whose consequence relation has a particularly strong, reversible connection with an equational semantics.
A method using theories of a logic and a quotient of its formula algebra to construct a semantic countermodel when a conclusion is not derivable.
A logic class defined by whether its Leibniz operator has useful behavior, including protoalgebraic and equivalential logics.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a consequence relation more informative than a list of theorems?
What is gained by treating a formula as an algebraic term?
Why can two logics with the same algebraic counterpart still have different logical properties?
How do soundness and completeness differ, and why are both needed?
What might be lost when a logic is modeled only by one designated value rather than a set or family of designated values?

summaries.example: Suppose a school rule says: “If a student has a library pass, then the student may borrow a book.” Let p mean “Mia has a library pass” and q mean “Mia may borrow a book.” A logic may say that p and p → q together support q. But different logics can disagree about what else follows. In a modal logic, □p might mean “p holds in every situation being considered.” Having p in the current situation does not always give □p. This helps explain why local and global modal consequence are different.
summaries.summary: The entry explains how propositional logics can be studied through algebra. It begins with abstract consequence relations: formal rules describing when a conclusion follows from premises. These include keeping premises available, allowing additional premises, and chaining deductions. When the relation is finitary, every consequence depends on some finite group of premises. A propositional logic adds a formal language and requires substitution invariance, so an argument pattern remains valid when its variables are replaced by other formulas. The source surveys classical, intuitionistic, modal, intuitionistic linear, and relevance logics. It then presents the algebraic viewpoint. Each connective is interpreted as an operation on an algebra, and each formula receives a value. In a logical matrix, some values are designated; a conclusion is acceptable when every valuation that designates the premises also designates the conclusion. Algebraic semantics is a more specific arrangement in which the designated values are uniformly described by equations. Classical logic is associated with Boolean algebras, and intuitionistic logic with Heyting algebras. The Lindenbaum-Tarski method turns theories into quotient algebras and is used to prove completeness results. A logic is algebraizable when formulas and equations can be translated back and forth in a strong, systematic way. The entry also distinguishes the algebraic counterpart of a logic from an algebraic semantics and explains that not every logic is algebraizable. The contrast between local and global normal modal logic K shows why the full consequence relation matters: the systems can share theorems and an algebraic counterpart while differing in what follows from premises. key_ideas: Tarski’s approach describes consequence generally: premises are kept, adding premises cannot remove consequences, and consequences of consequences remain consequences.
A logic is structural when replacing its variables uniformly with other formulas preserves consequence.
Classical logic uses truth valuations; intuitionistic logic, modal logics, linear logic, and relevance logic use different systems of rules or interpretations.
Algebraic logic interprets formulas as terms and connectives as operations, making logical reasoning available for algebraic study.
A matrix can use several designated values, which is useful when one special value cannot capture a logic’s behavior.
Some logics are algebraizable, but others are not. The source uses local and global modal K to show that similar-looking systems may have different consequence relations and properties.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic connects philosophical questions about valid reasoning with precise mathematical tools. It helps students see why a proof system, a model, and a consequence relation are different parts of logic. It also explains why non-classical logics are not simply mistakes or weakened versions of classical logic: they may be designed around different rules and semantic structures.

important_terms.definition: A rule for deciding which conclusions follow from a collection of starting statements.
A formal language built from variables, constants, and connectives such as and, or, and if-then.
A change that replaces variables by formulas while keeping the same overall pattern.
A mathematical structure that gives operations to the connectives of a logical language.
An algebra together with a set of values treated as acceptable for testing premises and conclusions.
A semantic description that is both sound and complete for a logic: it agrees with all and only the logical consequences.
A logic with a very strong two-way relationship to an algebraic semantics, allowing formulas and equations to translate into one another.

questions_to_think_about: Why should a logic respect a substitution that preserves the pattern of an argument?
What is the difference between a theorem and a consequence drawn from premises?
Why might a logic need several designated values instead of one?
How could a model show that a conclusion is not forced by its premises?
Why might the same algebraic class be connected with two logics that behave differently?
